endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: However, all mammograms are ultimately interpreted by the radiologist regardless of risk score.

endorsements.title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement
endorsements.issuer: ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR, RSNA; Radiol Artif Intell 2024 (PMID 38251899, doi:10.1148/ryai.230513)
endorsements.quote: The patient implications of decision making required in clinical medical imaging, even declarations of stability or normality, often have dramatic direct implications on patient care, which we suspect will require human co-supervision for some time.

endorsements.title: Artificial intelligence in medicine: has the time come to hang up the stethoscope?
endorsements.quote: So, while radiologists need to interpret all assigned cases per their standard of care, they can rely on notifications to prioritise.

endorsements.title: Pathology in the artificial intelligence era: Guiding innovation and implementation to preserve human insight
endorsements.quote: Key strategies include mandating explainability in AI systems, requiring continual human oversight for critical diagnostic tasks, and instituting iterative validation processes to ensure alignment with clinical and ethical standards.

evidence.title: Transforming Non-Digital, Clinical Workflows to Detect and Track Vision-Threatening Diabetic Retinopathy via a Digital Platform Integrating Artificial Intelligence: Implementation Research
evidence.outcome: Missed referrals identified through specialist review of AI-negative cases and subsequent referral attendance
evidence.effect: Specialist over-reading identified 1.13% FN (5/444); all were contacted and 80% (4/5) attended tertiary care. Over-reading, rather than adjudicated ground truth, defined false negatives.
evidence.quote: There were only 1.13% FN (5/444); all of them were contacted and 80% (4/5) presented at TC.

evidence.title: Standalone AI Versus AI-Assisted Radiologists in Emergency ICH Detection: A Prospective, Multicenter Diagnostic Accuracy Study
evidence.outcome: Radiologist review catching ICH cases missed (labeled negative) by AI
evidence.effect: All 45 ICH cases missed by AI were diagnosed by radiologists; AI missed 4.09% vs radiologists 1.09%.
evidence.quote: Conversely, in all 45 CT studies where AI services did not detect hemorrhages, pathology was identified by radiologists.

evidence.title: Real-world diagnostic performance of artificial intelligence in skin cancer screening
evidence.outcome: Cancers missed among lesions AI deemed benign that would be discharged without human review
evidence.effect: In lesions the AI deemed benign and that would have been discharged with no human review, four cancers were diagnosed.
evidence.quote: In lesions that the AI deemed benign, and that would have been discharged with no human review, four cancers were diagnosed.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence in emergency skeletal X-ray: post-deployment monitoring and clinical impact of incorrect AI results
evidence.outcome: Premature discharge caught by subsequent radiologist report
evidence.effect: Only one patient requiring treatment was prematurely discharged; recalled for treatment after the radiologist's report.
evidence.quote: Notably, the AI-assisted workflow only led to premature discharge of one patient who required treatment, and this patient was recalled to hospital for treatment following the radiologist's report.

evidence.title: Clinical Implementation of AI for Pulmonary Embolism Detection in over 30 000 CT Pulmonary Angiography Examinations
evidence.outcome: Radiologist interpretation of all cases alongside AI; unique PE diagnoses by radiologist vs AI alone
evidence.effect: Unique diagnosis by radiologist 483 of 3226 (14.97%), about 19 times AI alone (26 of 3226, 0.81%).
evidence.quote: The rate of unique diagnosis by the interpreting radiologist (483 of 3226 [14.97%]) was approximately 19 times that of the AI tool alone (26 of 3226 [0.81%]).

evidence.title: Identification of Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis Among Patients With Positive Interferon-Gamma Release Assay Results: Value of a Deep Learning-based Computer-aided Detection System in Different Scenarios of Implementation
evidence.outcome: Prescreening versus radiologist interpretation of all cases
evidence.effect: Specificity 88.8% vs. 85.7% (P <0.001) at same sensitivity; workload reduced 85.2% (1780 to 263).
evidence.quote: The CAD-based prescreening exhibited a higher specificity than the radiologists' interpretation (88.8% vs. 85.7%; P <0.001) at the same sensitivity, with a workload reduction of 85.2% (1780 to 263).

evidence.title: Collaborative strategies for deploying artificial intelligence to complement physician diagnoses of acute respiratory distress syndrome
evidence.outcome: Accuracy when physicians review only AI-uncertain cases versus all cases
evidence.effect: Physician review of only 20.8% of X-rays gave accuracy 0.869, near the weighted average requiring review of all (0.871); AI-only 0.847. Accuracy fell to 0.596 for AI in AI-uncertain cases.
evidence.quote: The weighted average of physician and AI model only marginally exceeded that of the physician-aided AI strategy, and would require physicians to review every chest X-ray.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence for detection of intracranial haemorrhage on head computed tomography scans: diagnostic accuracy in Hong Kong
evidence.venue: Hong Kong medical journal = Xianggang yi xue za zhi
evidence.outcome: False-negative scans before vs after manual review of model-nominated CT slices
evidence.effect: 22 false-negative scans reduced to six false-negative scans by manual review of the five model-nominated slices.
evidence.quote: There were 62 true-positive scans and 22 false-negative scans, which could be reduced to six false-negative scans by manual review of model-nominated CT slices.

evidence.title: Use of artificial intelligence in triaging of chest radiographs to reduce radiologists' workload
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity when the AI-ranked lower 50% of radiographs were treated as negative without radiologist review versus reading all
evidence.effect: Sensitivity was 82.6% reading all without DLD and 83.5% in the 50% worklist reduction scenario; difference 0.8% (95% CI -3.8% to 5.5%), noninferior. Specificity rose from 86.7% to 90.4%.
evidence.quote: The difference in sensitivity was 0.8% (95% CI: - 3.8%, 5.5%), establishing noninferiority of 50% worklist reduction (p = 0.01).

evidence.title: Geometric and dosimetric evaluation for breast and regional nodal auto-segmentation structures
evidence.venue: Journal of applied clinical medical physics
evidence.outcome: Need for clinician review of AI contours for post-mastectomy chestwall and IMN
evidence.effect: AC post-mastectomy CW and IMN showed dosimetric disagreement (IMN V90% significant; only 62.5% AC-CWs met ΔV95%<5%), so careful review is recommended; AxN and SC may need manual adjustment.
evidence.quote: Careful review should be performed for AC post-mastectomy CW and IMN before treatment planning.

evidence.title: Comparison of AI-integrated pathways with human-AI interaction in population mammographic screening for breast cancer
evidence.outcome: Performance of AI band-pass pathway where AI makes final decisions without human read
evidence.effect: AI band-pass without human reads for high/low scores gave 81.7% sensitivity, 96.6% specificity vs 79.8%/96.0% standard, with 80.7% fewer human reads; authors note lack of human decision-maker faces adoption challenges.
evidence.quote: However, having an AI reader make the final reading decision, without human involvement, faces challenges before clinical adoption.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence for Low-Dose CT Lung Cancer Screening: Comparison of Utilization Scenarios
evidence.outcome: clinician review of all cases
evidence.effect: Prescreener: per-nodule sensitivity 62.9% vs 64.2% (p = .16); specificity 90.3% vs 88.8% (p = .04); time 143 vs 164 seconds.
evidence.quote: An approach whereby radiologists only interpret LDCT examinations with a positive AI result can reduce radiologists' workload while preserving sensitivity.

evidence.title: AI for fracture diagnosis in clinical practice: Four approaches to systematic AI-implementation and their impact on AI-effectiveness
evidence.outcome: Missed fractures when AI triages cases versus radiologist reviewing all cases
evidence.effect: AI-triage (radiologist findings consulted only when AI in doubt) increased FN to 2.1% (32/1508) vs radiologist 2.7% overall, but increased FN in all subgroups except radiologists-in-training.
evidence.quote: Subgroups show similar trends, except AI-triage increased FN for all subgroups except radiologists-in-training.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence in population breast cancer screening: A two-year cost-effectiveness analysis
evidence.outcome: missed cancers when low-risk mammograms lacked human reading
evidence.effect: Triage Only saved $4/person but detected 0.521 fewer cancers per 1000 vs standard; ICER $8206 per additional cancer detected.
evidence.quote: In the base-case analysis, Triage Only was the most efficient strategy, saving an average of $4 per person screened but detecting 0.521 fewer cancers per 1000 people screened compared to standard practice (ICER $8206 per additional cancer detected).

evidence.title: Evaluating Artificial Intelligence as a First-Pass Reader in Fundus Photograph Screening: A Multireader Workflow Validation Study
evidence.outcome: AI false-negative correction
evidence.effect: False-negative correction: AMD 2–20/67 (3–30%); DR 17–20/37 (46–54%); RVO 0–1/2, despite human review/arbitration.
evidence.quote: Correction of standalone AI false negatives was less consistent (AMD, 2–20 of 67 [3–30%]; DR, 17–20 of 37 [46–54%]; RVO, 0–1 of 2) ( Table S3 ).

evidence.title: Evaluating an AI-assisted triage workflow for retinal diseases
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity for DR and AMD when AI-negative images skip clinician review versus human-only reading
evidence.effect: DR sensitivity fell 0.9168 to 0.8838 (diff -0.0330; p<0.001); AMD 0.8570 to 0.8445 (diff -0.0124; p=0.008); ophthalmologist review reduced to 7.3%-16.8% of images.
evidence.quote: For DR, mean sensitivity decreased from 0.9168 to 0.8838 (difference, -0.0330; 95% CI, -0.0495 to -0.0165; p < 0.001), whereas the increase in specificity did not reach statistical significance.

evidence.title: Impact of real-life use of artificial intelligence as support for human reading in a population-based breast cancer screening program with mammography and tomosynthesis
evidence.outcome: Detected cancers assigned low risk by AI
evidence.effect: Among 108 detected cancers, AI categorized 1 (0.9%) as low risk, 32 (29.6%) as intermediate, and 75 (69.4%) as elevated.
evidence.quote: The 108 studies with cancers were categorized as follows: low, 1 (0.9%); intermediate, 32 (29.6%); elevated, 75 (69.4%) (Fig. 4 ).
evidence.sample_unit: women (screening examinations; 11,998 AI-supported and 11,998 matched historical controls)

evidence.title: Towards clinical implementation of an AI-algorithm for detection of cervical spine fractures on computed tomography
evidence.outcome: Fractures missed by AI prioritization tool, and their clinical relevance
evidence.effect: 22 fractures missed by AI, of which 5 required stabilizing therapy; sensitivity 89.8% (95% CI 84.2-94.0%), NPV 99.1%.
evidence.quote: 22 fractures were missed by AI of which 5 required stabilizing therapy.

evidence.title: Real-World Performance of Pneumothorax-Detecting Artificial Intelligence Algorithm and its Impact on Radiologist Reporting Times
evidence.outcome: AI sensitivity for pneumothorax in real-world inpatient CXRs
evidence.effect: Overall AUC .78, sensitivity .60, specificity .97; for moderate/large PTx AUC .93, sensitivity .89, specificity .96
evidence.quote: Area under ROC curve (AUC) for the AI tool was.78 with sensitivity of .60 and specificity of .97.

evidence.title: Automated detection of superior mesenteric artery occlusion on post-contrast CT Using a 3D deep learning model
evidence.outcome: Findings missed on initial radiologist read and identified by AI QA review
evidence.effect: Of 237 QA-flagged cases, 83 (35.0%) were confirmed missed SMAO, indicating 40.7% of SMAO cases were undiagnosed on the initial read.
evidence.quote: The model flagged 237 cases for QA review, of which 83 (35.0%) were confirmed as missed SMAO, indicating that 40.7% of SMAO cases were undiagnosed on the initial read.

evidence.title: Prospective Shadow-Mode Evaluation of an Artificial Intelligence Tool for Intracranial Aneurysm Detection on CT Angiography: Incremental Yield and Operational Impact
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
evidence.outcome: Aneurysms detected by radiologists but missed by AI
evidence.effect: Radiologist-only aneurysms were mostly 3 to 5 mm (18 of 33, 54.5%); AI-alone sensitivity was 0.846, 0.787-0.894.
evidence.quote: Most AI-only aneurysms were <3 mm (31 of 55, 56.4%); radiologist-only were mostly 3 to 5 mm (18 of 33, 54.5%).

evidence.title: Validation and three years of clinical experience in using an artificial intelligence algorithm as a second read system for prostate cancer diagnosis-real-world experience
evidence.outcome: False-negative cancer findings in slides labeled benign by AI
evidence.effect: AI called nine cancer slides benign; seven were GG1, and the other two were GG2 and GG4. No cancers were missed at the case level out of 1279 WSI.

evidence.title: Post-deployment performance of a deep learning algorithm for normal and abnormal chest X-ray classification: A study at visa screening centers in the United Arab Emirates
evidence.outcome: Missed abnormal findings among CXRs the AI classified as normal (negative predictive value vs radiologists)

evidence.title: Use of natural language processing to identify patients with inflammatory breast cancer across a health-care system

evidence.quote: Of 255 confirmed paients with inflammatory breast cancer in this cohort, our NLP plus human-in-the-loop system correctly identified 235 cases (true positives), missing 20 cases (false negatives), yielding a sensitivity of 92.2%.

evidence.title: Incidental pulmonary embolism in abdominal CT: detection rate and characteristics with artificial intelligence

commentary.bottom_line: Sixteen studies test whether clinicians should read every case regardless of AI triage, and their results split: real-deployment studies show human readers catching AI misses, while several simulations report that skipping low-priority cases kept sensitivity similar and cut workload. The evidence supports human review of AI-negative cases as a way to catch misses, but it does not show that reviewing every case outperforms well-validated partial review in patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: Of 16 studies, 9 favor the practice, 4 oppose it, and 3 are mixed. Three prospective real-deployment studies favor it, but none randomized readers or measured patient outcomes. Eleven studies are offline or simulated, and five come from real deployment. One study defined false negatives by the over-read itself. Inconsistency and indirectness lower certainty to low.

Radiologists diagnosed all 45 hemorrhages the AI missed, and review of lesions the AI deemed benign found four cancers. Review does not guarantee a catch. Readers who kept AI results missed 33.0% of AI-false-negative cases versus 2.7% without AI, and reviewers corrected 3% to 30% of AI misses for macular degeneration.

Simulations report that prescreening cut workload by 85.2% with higher specificity. A 50% worklist cut kept sensitivity noninferior (difference 0.8%). Reading time fell from 164 to 143 seconds. In a fracture study, AI triage raised false negatives for every reader subgroup except trainees, so the effect may depend on who reads.

The authors of an Australian band-pass study, where AI made final calls on high and low scores, reported that the lack of a human decision-maker poses adoption challenges. This suggests that current oversight expectations favor human review, even where simulated accuracy was similar to standard reading.

In Thailand, specialist over-reading found 5 missed referrals among 444 AI-negative cases, and 4 of those 5 patients attended tertiary care after being contacted. In Norway, one prematurely discharged patient was recalled for treatment after the radiologist's report. These cases suggest that human review gives patients a route back to care.

No test of the practice reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The hazard studies include a Puerto Rico pathology deployment, where AI called nine cancer slides benign, and a Medicaid message-triage study, where no autonomous benchmark was met. These studies show the hazard exists in these groups but do not test the safeguard.

commentary.research_gap: No study randomized sites or readers to universal review versus AI-triaged partial review with patient outcomes such as delayed diagnosis or harm as endpoints. Studies are also needed that measure automation bias during universal review and that report results by reader experience.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the 16 studies testing the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Only hazard studies touched these groups, so it is unknown whether universal review catches AI misses at the same rate in safety-net settings.
